Last fall, on my birthday trip, I went to Devil’s Lake, and quietly decided I’d come back again this summer.
Today, on a whim, we took a half-day trip to Devil’s Lake. In summer, Devil’s Lake has bright, crisp colors and is packed with people. Lots of families brought all kinds of fancy hammocks, umbrellas, and grills, chatting and picnicking by the lake; quite a few others paddled kayaks out to the middle of the lake to fish, enjoying a quiet moment to themselves. As for us, we walked trails along the west side of the lake, out and back.
On the way there, we took the Tumbled Rocks Trail. The clouds smoothed over the dip in the hills across the lake like a layer of butter, so lovely. On the way back, we tackled the West Bluff Trail, which meant climbing over a small hill, but the view from the top was gorgeous, the lake and sky reflecting each other, well worth the climb.
I wonder what the lake looks like in winter and spring. If I get the chance, I’d love to see all four of its seasonal faces.

A few weeks ago I ordered a miniature house kit. Sam and I spent ten nights building it together. I recorded our daily progress along with close-ups of the finished sushi restaurant in the video below!
I was a bit rattled when the package arrived: the box had gotten pretty banged up in transit. But I couldn’t be bothered to return it, so we just dove straight into building, and right up until the very last piece we were both worried something might be missing. Thankfully, every single part was in the box, and it even came with tweezers, though we had to supply our own scissors and white glue.
The most fun part was making the sushi! For the nigiri, both the fish and the rice were made out of felt. We’d glue two pieces of felt together, cut them into a long strip with scissors, and then snip that into bite-sized pieces. For the nori rolls, we’d back the felt with black paper first, then actually roll it up the way you’d roll real sushi. Once the food was made and set on the plates, the final touch was sprinkling on green powder for wasabi, yellow powder for pickled ginger, and some red powder whose exact flavor I still can’t identify.
So cute, right?
The piece that frustrated me most was the sake bottle from day five, especially the one with the character “濤” written on it. The bottle itself was a hollow bead, and we had to glue a toothpick into the center of the bead to create a protruding effect, then wrap it in gold foil, and finally tie it up with string and knot it. Every single step was maddeningly difficult: either the toothpick would slip out of place, or the knot just wouldn’t hold. It took forever, but we finally got through it.
On the nights we worked on the miniature, it felt like stepping into the Room of Spirit and Time: time would just fly by. Building the model wasn’t just a great way to zone out; every so often, some strangely profound thought would surface too. One night, while wrestling with some tiny piece in my hands, I suddenly remembered this verse: “We are the clay, you are the potter; we are all the work of your hand.” I felt like I could understand, just a little, what that might feel like from God’s side.
If one day my salmon nigiri got full of itself and turned to the tuna nigiri next to it and said, “Ha, I’m way better than you,” I’d probably scoop it right off the plate and send it to stand in the corner and think about what it did.
And if my little plant piece put itself down and said, “The restaurant would be better off without me,” I’d probably say, quite sadly, but I cut you out leaf by leaf with my own hands: the restaurant wouldn’t be complete without you!
If that’s how I feel, how much more must God feel the same way.

This post discusses plot details from Dream of the Red Chamber. If you’d rather avoid spoilers, please don’t read on.
Preface Halfway through Dream of the Red Chamber! Once you commit to a serialized column, you realize keeping up with it really isn’t easy: I really want to fall behind on deadlines.
First, I want to add a bit to something I mentioned in the last installment: that the main throughline of Dream of the Red Chamber is watching Bao-yu and Dai-yu fall in love. I’m a little worried that gave readers the impression that Cao Xueqin spends huge stretches of the book on the two of them interacting directly, but that’s actually not quite true. At least across the first sixty chapters, Cao Xueqin spends a lot of time narrating the interactions of plenty of other characters too, weaving them into every link of the Jia family’s story, using these characters to display the full range of human experience, letting readers look down on the different directions different people choose to pursue in life.
Maybe, more than romantic love as a theme, what Cao Xueqin is really more focused on is the question of “what actually counts as a life worth pursuing.”
Quick recap of key plot points, Chapters 41-60 Xi-feng catches Jia Lian and Bao-er’s wife in bed together; Dai-yu and Bao-chai reconcile; Faithful refuses, to the death, to marry Jia She; Xi-feng, recovering from a miscarriage, hands off household management to Lady Wang, Li Wan, and Tan-chun; Bao-yu is scared half out of his wits by a joke Nightingale plays on him.
What actually counts as a life worth pursuing? For every character in the story, the answer is different: for some it’s the purest form of love, for others it’s absolute power, for others it’s peaceful relationships. Whatever it is, the person pursuing it first has to assume that thing is real, not illusory. That premise has to hold before there’s any motivation to chase after it at all. And yet in Dream of the Red Chamber, Cao Xueqin deliberately blurs the line between what’s real and what’s illusory, in a couplet that could be paraphrased as: treat the false as true, and the true turns false as well; treat nothingness as something, and something turns, in the end, back to nothing.
This couplet is what Jia Bao-yu reads early in the story during his dream-journey through the Land of Illusion, and it also serves as the central theme of the entire novel: illusion may well reflect reality, and what you believe to be real may well be false. Working from that premise, we find that the “illusory” dream sequences become the author’s tool for foreshadowing the “real” ending, for instance, the Second Supplementary Register of the Twelve Beauties of Jinling that Bao-yu reads in his dream, whose verses actually describe the tragic fates awaiting several of the young women of Prospect Garden. On the flip side, the “real” life depicted in the story ends up reading like a fleeting dream itself: scenes like everyone huddling together to compose poetry and grill meat together in the snow carry a sense of being almost too good to be real.
Even though readers may pick up on this, the characters within the story don’t: even after Bao-yu and Wang Xi-feng each experience prophetic dreams, neither of them really grasps what those dreams mean. Once they wake, they go right back to living in blissful ignorance of what’s coming, laughing as much as they want, crying as much as they want, chasing after whatever their hearts desire without restraint. For Bao-yu and Dai-yu, sincerity of feeling is what matters most, and they don’t care whether the rest of the world approves or not. For Wang Xi-feng, the image of the unbreakable powerhouse woman must be maintained at all costs: even after a miscarriage brought on by chronic overwork leaves her body severely weakened, she still puts up a strong front in front of others. For Lady Xing (Wang Xi-feng’s mother-in-law), her husband’s word is absolute law: even when her husband, Jia She, asks her to help him find a concubine, she does it without a moment’s hesitation.
Sounds pretty absurd, right? But maybe that’s exactly the effect Cao Xueqin was going for: using other people’s absurdity as a mirror, prompting us to ask ourselves whether the values we hold onto so tightly are actually real, and whether they’re really worth pouring everything we have into pursuing.
Is the ultimate truth of life really tragedy? That said, it’s worth noting that this novel is, at its core, a tragedy: the dream sequences you assume are illusory turn out to foreshadow a genuinely tragic ending, while the beauty you assume is real ultimately amounts to nothing. Either way, beauty is never eternal, and illusion and emptiness are, in the end, what life’s truth really comes down to. Perhaps the author’s own lament on this is hidden in Dai-yu’s view on banquets: wherever people gather, they must eventually part, and however joyful the gathering, doesn’t the parting that follows only bring on a chill and a sadness? So maybe it’s better never to gather at all. She likens it to flowers: they delight us when they bloom, but only bring more heartache once they wither, so maybe it would be better if they never bloomed in the first place.
(Wait, doesn’t this basically boil down to: since you’re going to get hungry again eventually, wouldn’t it be better not to eat at all?)
As much as I like Dai-yu as a character, I don’t actually agree with her view here. Just as she believes gathering isn’t the whole of life, the sorrow of parting isn’t the whole of life either. The experience of people coming together is a lot like eating: sure, the meal eventually ends, but the food gets converted into nourishment (or, well, waste), bringing nourishment (or occasionally harm) that turns you into a slightly different person (hopefully healthier, or possibly just running to the bathroom more often).
And besides, if the ultimate truth of life really is tragedy and emptiness, then why do most of us still feel this urge to work hard, to long for good relationships, to chase after something? Is the belief that life is fundamentally tragic something we hold simply because we’ve been hurt? Just as Dai-yu’s view comes directly from having lost both her parents. Is a view shaped by pain automatically the absolute truth? If she had instead been born into a happy family, and had instead declared: precisely because gatherings and partings are part of life, we should cherish the present all the more, could that, too, have become just as valid a truth?
Our beliefs about the ultimate truth of life are shaped by our past experiences, and those beliefs, in turn, determine how we live our lives now.
I’ve wandered a bit far afield here. Even though I don’t agree with the author’s underlying view that “life is ultimately a tragedy,” I do think it’s genuinely interesting how, through these characters, he pushes readers to reconsider whether the lives we pursue are actually real and actually worth pursuing. Maybe we all need to stop and reconsider: behind the things we work so hard to chase in daily life, what values do they actually represent, and is there any chance those values are illusory too?
In Summary The more I read, the more I find myself unable to resist the charm of every single character, even knowing full well the story is headed toward tragedy! It’s a feeling a lot like: you finally get close with everyone in your class, even the classmate you had a little friction with turns out to have her own lovable side, and then you realize graduation is just a year away QAQ.
Ugh, and now I’m starting to see the household servants stirring up trouble too. Could this be the first sign of the tragedy to come? To find out what happens next, stay tuned for the next installment.

Baotan (爆炭, “exploding charcoal”): describes a fiery, hot temper. Example sentence: “That little wretch Skybright has a temper like exploding charcoal.” A wonderfully vivid image! You can practically picture Skybright’s temper crackling and popping like burning charcoal. “Opened a fruit stand”: beaten black and blue, skin broken and bleeding, like the riot of colors in a fruit stand’s produce. Example sentence: “Xiang-lian walked over to take a look, and realizing he (Xue Pan) wasn’t used to taking a beating, only used about thirty percent of his strength, giving his face a few slaps, and just like that, he’d ‘opened a fruit stand.’” A pretty funny metaphor: in modern terms, you’d basically say his face “opened up its own fruit shop." Hehezhezhe (蝎蝎螫螫): describes being excessively anxious, timid, and easily fussed. Shixin (“solid heart”): sincere, earnest. Example sentence: “Don’t go saying he (Bao-yu) is just some sincere, foolish child.” A pretty interesting descriptor: so does that mean if someone’s got a lot of twists and turns going on inside them, you could call them “hollow-hearted”? lol Dream of the Red Chamber series [Auntie Reads the Red Chamber] The Jia Household, Teetering: Chapters 1-20 [Auntie Reads the Red Chamber] Entangled Hearts Among Bao-yu, Dai-yu, and Bao-chai: Chapters 21-40

This post discusses plot details from Dream of the Red Chamber. If you’d rather avoid spoilers, please don’t read on.
Preface I’ve finally made it to chapter forty! Once you commit to a column, you’ve got to keep serializing it: I felt like if I let it sit too long I’d get lazy and lose the will to write, so I’ve been pushing myself to read a bit and write a bit, keeping pace. These twenty chapters delivered a lot of iconic scenes, including Dai-yu burying the fallen blossoms, and Grannie Liu’s visit to Prospect Garden, the one that shows up in middle school textbooks. This time around, I want to talk about the two female leads, Lin Dai-yu and Xue Bao-chai.
Quick recap of key plot points, Chapters 21-40 Bao-yu and his sisters and cousins move into Prospect Garden; Dai-yu buries the fallen blossoms; Jia Zheng nearly beats Bao-yu to death; a poetry club is formed; Grannie Liu visits Prospect Garden.
Dai-yu Sam asked me what the main plot of Dream of the Red Chamber actually is, and I said: it’s just watching all these siblings fall in love! (“Watching a great family decline” would’ve been way too dry an answer, who’d want to read that!) Bao-yu and Dai-yu are basically the male and female leads of a romance drama: gorgeous, constantly falling into misunderstandings, sulking, finally patching things up only to suddenly realize the other person is their true soulmate, then endlessly testing each other’s feelings all over again. If that’s not a romance drama, what is?
Even though Cao Xueqin gives a fatalistic, predestined explanation for why Dai-yu cries so much, I want to first try understanding her tendency toward melancholy from a purely human angle. Of the three (Bao-yu, Dai-yu, and Bao-chai), Dai-yu is the youngest, Bao-yu is in the middle, and Bao-chai is the oldest. Dai-yu lost both her parents at a very young age (probably around middle-school age), and coming face to face with death is a life-altering thing for anyone, let alone a little girl her age. On top of that, her health is frail and she’s frequently unwell; her own father died of illness. For her, death often feels like it’s lurking right at the door, as if it could swallow her whole at any moment, so expecting her to be a cheerful, carefree kid is honestly not very realistic. Add to that the fact that she has to live with her uncle’s entire extended household, which only means more friction and more chances to rub people the wrong way. She isn’t especially confident in herself, and her personality tends toward the earnest and serious side, and life really is hard for her.
Watching this frail yet brilliantly talented girl in her tentative, blossoming romance with our wealthy young master, I couldn’t help but let out an involuntary little chuckle of an “aunty smile” as a reader. Take this moment: Dai-yu hears that Bao-yu has been out visiting all day, and grows anxious, sending someone to check on him two or three times that evening; the moment she learns he’s been scalded, she drops everything and hurries over herself. When the person you love gets hurt, Dai-yu’s concern comes through loud and clear! And when Bao-yu drops by her room and overhears her talking to herself, Dai-yu, mortified at having let her feelings slip, blushes without meaning to, pulls her sleeve over her face, and turns to the wall, pretending to be asleep. Doesn’t that just make you think Dai-yu is unbearably cute? And this same adorable Dai-yu even has a farm-girl look in her wardrobe! When she goes to bury the fallen blossoms, her outfit actually reminded me of Li Wei, the female lead from the drama My Journey to You, dressed head to toe like a farm girl, and yet somehow still coming across completely clean and utterly adorable.
Dai-yu and Bao-yu are clearly drawn to each other. So far, Dai-yu is the only one who can reach that place deep inside Bao-yu that aches over the passing of time and mourns the fading of spring, and she’s also the only one who never once tells him to go work hard and chase after worldly success and status. That’s exactly why Bao-yu loves her. Even though, deep down, they both quietly recognize each other as soulmates, the aimlessness of youth still keeps tangling them up. What makes things hard between them isn’t just that they both tend to say the opposite of what they mean whenever things get the slightest bit romantic; it’s also the far heavier weight of the fated “match of gold and jade.”
Cao Xueqin never has the narrator directly explain what this “match of gold and jade” actually means. Instead, he lets the reader piece it together through the characters’ own conversations: Bao-yu was born with a piece of jade in his mouth, and Bao-chai owns a gold locket, given to her by a monk, who told her that one day she would marry a young man born with jade. Everyone already knows this story, and everyone has quietly already assumed Bao-yu and Bao-chai will end up together. Because of this, for Dai-yu, even once she’s certain that Bao-yu really is her soulmate, that sense of fatalism still keeps her from ever letting herself express her feelings for him without reservation, because every banquet eventually has to end, so maybe it’s better not to have happy memories to lose in the first place. Reading this part, I understood a bit better why Bao-yu is always throwing his jade around and smashing it, because that “spiritual jade” feels like a “perfect match” he can never break free of or destroy, something everyone else thinks is wonderful, but which, for him, is really just a shackle trapping him away from what his heart actually wants.
So really, you can’t blame Dai-yu for crying so much: she has her own reasons, and her own pain, that she just can’t help.
Bao-chai As the second female lead of this romance drama, Bao-chai carries a maturity and worldliness well beyond her fifteen years. Like Dai-yu, she lost her father early, though her mother is still alive, so she’s come to depend on the Jia household along with her mother and older brother, Xue Pan. Even though she’s technically the younger sister, Xue Pan really doesn’t act much like an older brother (he lazes around all day doing nothing), which has left Bao-chai’s personality shaped more like an older sister’s. And since she’s also the eldest of the three among Bao-yu, Dai-yu, and herself, Bao-yu and Dai-yu end up feeling almost like her own younger brother and sister. On top of that, Bao-chai, like Dai-yu, is genuinely talented with words, but where Dai-yu leans romantic, Bao-chai’s personality is more grounded and practical, much like her own room, which has almost no decoration and is entirely focused on function.
Bao-chai is extremely well-liked within the Jia household: her emotional intelligence and social skills are both remarkably high, and she has a real gift for being considerate of other people’s feelings. She’s sharply aware of how her own words and actions land on others. Once, when Grandmother Jia asks what she likes, Bao-chai, knowing full well that the old woman loves lively opera and sweet, soft food, tailors her answer accordingly, which only makes the old woman like her even more. Another time, she’s about to go find Dai-yu, but notices Bao-yu has gotten there first, so she quietly turns and leaves instead, not wanting to make either of them uncomfortable. Bao-chai’s habit of thinking of others comes as naturally to her as eating or drinking water. It never feels like she’s deliberately trying to please anyone. If I had to name someone who deliberately tries to please people, I’d think of Jia Zheng instead: Cao Xueqin repeatedly uses the verb “smiling ingratiatingly” whenever describing Jia Zheng trying to curry favor with someone, but he never once describes Bao-chai that way.
Having read up through chapter forty, the question I find myself most curious about is this: does this endlessly considerate Bao-chai actually have feelings for Bao-yu? From the clues so far, it seems like she might just think of him as a little brother. As the female lead of the “match of gold and jade,” she obviously knows about the prophecy, and yet her instinct is to actively keep her distance from Bao-yu. She even seems unimpressed when she notices Bao-yu’s older sister Yuan-chun sent her the exact same gift as Bao-yu, and she sometimes teases Bao-yu and Dai-yu about their close, childhood-sweetheart-style bond. That said, when she overhears Bao-yu mumbling in his sleep, insisting he doesn’t believe in the “match of gold and jade” but only in the “match of wood and stone,” Bao-chai still visibly freezes up. My current guess is that she doesn’t have romantic feelings for Bao-yu at all. She probably really does just see him as a little brother, and probably treats the whole “match of gold and jade” business as more of a “well, since everyone says so, I guess that’s just how it is” kind of thing. She’s not especially fond of the idea either, but there doesn’t seem to be much need to actively refuse it, so as long as it keeps everyone happy, why not. I’m not sure if that guess is right or not. Let’s keep reading and find out.
Our Male Lead, Impossible Not to Roast I keep feeling like this wealthy young master, Bao-yu, has no idea just how much trouble his behavior causes other people, much of the time.
For instance, there’s a moment where he’s caught in the rain outside and comes home to Green Delights soaking wet, wanting to change clothes, and the maid inside takes forever to open the door. So he decides that whoever it is, he’s going to kick her the moment she opens up. Turns out it’s Aroma, the maid who takes the best care of him out of anyone, and without stopping to think, he kicks her right in the ribs, hard enough that she coughs up blood. He does feel bad about it afterward and takes good care of her, but honestly, this guy is a bit much.
Then there’s the incident where, without any sense of consequence, he flirts with Golden, his own mother’s maid. His mother, protecting her son, decides the maid must be the one at fault and has her dismissed. Somehow, Golden can’t get past it and ends up drowning herself in a well. Bao-yu, though upset, still turns around and asks Golden’s sister, Silver, whether their mother is doing okay, genuinely oblivious to how the world works. He was the one who indirectly caused her death, and here he is asking about her mother’s well-being.
And there’s more! When Bao-chai complains about the heat and skips out on watching an opera with everyone else, Bao-yu’s actual response is that no wonder people compare her to Lady Yang, since she’s on the plump side too. This guy actually dares to say something that disrespectful to a woman. It’s basically: “Oh, you feel hot? That must be because you’re fat!” So rude!! 😡😡🤬 And it gets worse: when he catches sight of Bao-chai’s snow-white arm, he can’t help but think to himself that if that arm belonged to Miss Lin, he might get to touch it, but of all people it had to be hers, which just proves how unlucky he is. If that’s not creepy, I don’t know what is.
In Summary Reading Dream of the Red Chamber, it’s pretty much unavoidable to end up either “Team Dai-yu” or “Team Bao-chai.” Care to guess which team I’m on?
Given how much enthusiasm I've clearly put into this, it's probably not hard to guess I'm Team Dai-yu! Dai-yu really is adorable, and even cuter when she's being prickly! That said, even though I’m Team Dai-yu, Jia Bao-yu is really not my type at all. Sam is still my number one ❤️ (unprompted PDA, sorry).
I think part of why I like her so much is that I see a version of my own middle-school self in her. Back then, I got emotional at the smallest things (okay, fine, I cried a lot), and I felt everything deeply when it came to life’s partings and its underlying sadness, and I wasn’t very good at processing complicated emotions, and I’d often get tangled up in my own head about things. But thankfully, I ran into some genuinely good people along the way (not that I never met bad ones, but the ratio was low), and, by some real stroke of luck, I made it through okay.
If I could ask for one thing, it would be for Dai-yu’s story not to end in tragedy, because that feeling would be too much like watching a younger version of myself, missing just a few crucial lamps along the way, wander down a road that leads to ruin. So looking back, I really do feel grateful for the people who lit my way through those dim years of youth, and helped me find a different path.
Finally, it feels like a tragic fate is quietly closing in on all three of them: Bao-yu, Dai-yu, and Bao-chai. What they say and do keeps foreshadowing how it will all end: Bao-yu says that if Dai-yu dies, he’ll become a monk; Dai-yu pushes Bao-yu away; and the poem Bao-chai writes seems to predict that her own marriage will be short-lived rather than lasting. How exactly do the three of them end up there? To find out what happens next, stay tuned for the next installment.
[Fun Vocabulary] Text in black is the definition, orange text is my own take on it.
Lieju (趔趄): to stagger, stumbling off-balance as if about to fall. Daiyan (“dumb goose”): a mocking term for someone acting dim-witted, like calling someone a “fool” or a “dunce.” This phrase made me think of that random goose I saw on the street a while back. Turns out, whether ancient or modern, everyone agrees geese just look kind of dopey. Futai: describes someone with a full, plump figure. Fat. “The Idle Master of Wealth and Leisure”: Jia Bao-yu’s nickname (pen name). The classical-era version of “rich and has way too much free time." Budangjiahuala (不當家花拉的): “budangjia” means “shouldn’t” or “what a sin,” and “huala” is a suffix, also said as “hualala” or “hualazi.” This construction follows basically the same logic as the modern phrase “well, that’s it, we’re cooked." This post discusses plot details from Dream of the Red Chamber. If you’d rather avoid spoilers, please don’t read on.
Preface A while back, while reading Sabrina Huang’s essays, I noticed she used some phrases that trace back to Dream of the Red Chamber, classical in origin yet surprisingly fresh. Something in me stirred, and I thought: why not take on the challenge of reading Dream of the Red Chamber myself?
I found the China Times Publishing edition of Dream of the Red Chamber, with a preface by Pai Hsien-yung, and detailed annotations for every chapter. Since I’m reading the ebook version, clicking a hyperlink jumps straight between the footnotes and the main text, instead of the whole flipping-back-and-forth ordeal a print book would require. On top of that, some of Cao Xueqin’s phrasing is fairly close to vernacular Chinese and isn’t too hard to follow. All together, it’s lowered the barrier to reading classical Chinese by quite a bit.
My original plan was to grind through all 120 chapters before writing up any thoughts, but that felt like way too much to take on at once: I was worried I’d lose all motivation to write by the time I got there. Then I remembered that the YouTuber JiuJiu Shoes once made a video series called “A Straight Guy Watches Empresses in the Palace,” and I thought, why not borrow that concept and turn it into a similar serialized column? Watching this cast of teenage siblings fall in love, and these little brats trash-talking and brawling in the schoolroom, I realized I actually needed to take a deep breath and be patient about it, and I really felt like part of me had gotten old. Guess the column name has to be “Auntie Reads the Red Chamber” then. Recording my gut reactions and reflections as I read Dream of the Red Chamber should be pretty interesting.
Quick recap of key plot points, Chapters 1-20 Lin Dai-yu arrives at the Jia household; Wang Xi-feng gets her revenge on Jia Rui; Ke-qing, Jia Rong’s wife, passes away; Prospect Garden is completed; Yuan-chun returns home to visit her family (Dai-yu passes a note, and Bao-chai secretly feeds Bao-yu answers while helping him write poems).
Jia Bao-yu My first impression of Jia Bao-yu is that he’s an extremely smooth-talking teenage brat. The very first thing he says to Lin Dai-yu is, “I’ve seen this sister somewhere before.” Then he immediately gives her a nickname, “Frowner” (a very teenage-boy move, giving people nicknames!). When he’s first introduced, there’s a passage describing him as wayward and perverse in temper, reckless of what the world might think of him, which honestly makes him sound like a bit of a scoundrel: he lazes around all day and isn’t much for studying, but he’s incredibly popular with women, because he’s endlessly sweet and attentive to every single one of them, always calling them “dear sister” or “dear cousin.”
Even though my first impression of Bao-yu wasn’t great, he does have a certain strange charm: he gives off the sense that he’d hand you his whole heart at any given moment. He doesn’t bother with propriety or rules, and his feelings are completely unfiltered. For instance: he doesn’t want his maid Aroma to go home, so he whines and clings to her over and over; when his friend Qin Zhong dies (even though Qin Zhong wasn’t exactly a great person either), he cries his heart out over it. He has his own theory about men and women (one of his famous lines: girls are made of the substance of water, and boys are made of the substance of mud; when he’s around girls he feels fresh and clean, but around men he feels like he’s choking on foulness), and he’s always drawn to hanging out with girls, not particularly caring what anyone else thinks.
On top of that, the way his mind works is sometimes genuinely mysterious. Everyone’s watching an opera and he finds it boring, so he wanders off to the study to look at a painting of a beautiful woman, because he figures the woman in the painting must be lonely too and needs him to go comfort her. Or take his first meeting with Dai-yu: he asks whether she, like him, was born with a piece of jade. She says no, and he suddenly flies into a rage and bursts into tears, hurling the jade he was born with onto the floor. Reading that, I honestly thought, is this guy okay? But looking at it from another angle, I think Bao-yu is basically someone terrified of loneliness, with an unusually distinctive personality: as a man, he enjoys all the privileges that come with being male, and yet he doesn’t like the traits typically expected of men, nor is he willing to follow the rules and social values that men have set up. Living under that kind of tension, it’s no wonder his feelings erupt in such strange places.
I thought I didn’t like Bao-yu, until his father, Jia Zheng, showed up, and I realized I couldn’t stand Jia Zheng even more.
Jia Zheng The father-son relationship between Bao-yu and Jia Zheng is a constant, high-tension standoff. The two of them sit at opposite ends of a spectrum: Jia Zheng is a scholar, while Bao-yu can’t stand studying; Jia Zheng is bound by countless rules, while Bao-yu’s personality is wild and unrestrained. The two don’t really interact much until Chapter 17, once Prospect Garden is finished being built. In that chapter, Jia Zheng, wanting to test his son’s talent, takes him and a group of hangers-on to tour the garden and name its various scenic spots and pavilions. Before this, Bao-yu was always avoiding his father as much as possible, terrified of being quizzed on his studies, so I’d more or less assumed he was completely useless academically. But it turns out the names Bao-yu comes up with for the garden’s spots are actually quite good, showing real literary talent, and yet his father is never satisfied. Not just unsatisfied, either: his father keeps calling him “beast, beast,” and keeps flip-flopping on what he wants: when Bao-yu talks too much, he accuses his son of showing off in front of the hangers-on; when Bao-yu, stung by the scolding, stops talking, he snaps at him for staying silent. This man is genuinely exhausting and difficult to deal with.
Jia Zheng’s rule-bound nature also comes through in his interactions with his daughter Yuan-chun. Yuan-chun, the eldest daughter, now an imperial consort, finally makes it home for a rare visit and speaks to her father from the heart, telling him that although she now lives in wealth and honor, being parted from her own flesh and blood leaves her, in the end, with no real joy in it. Jia Zheng responds with a long, relentlessly politically-correct speech, referring to himself as “your subject,” and telling his daughter to serve the Emperor well so as not to squander such great imperial favor, and so on. Yuan-chun has no choice but to fend him off with equally formal, bureaucratic language in return. I suspect what she was really thinking was: I finally got off work, so why do I have to keep working the second I get home?
I think Jia Zheng is, underneath it all, a deeply repressed person, and that repression is exactly what keeps him at such a distance from his children. My guess is that Jia Zheng might actually envy Bao-yu, at least a little. In Jia Zheng’s eyes, he himself has worked incredibly hard and lived an extremely “correct” life; meanwhile, his son is the type who was born extraordinary, gifted with talent, and doesn’t have to try particularly hard at anything, and on top of that, his mother (Bao-yu’s grandmother) dotes on him endlessly. The fact that Bao-yu’s “incorrectness” still brings him such a comfortable, easy life might be exactly what throws Jia Zheng so off balance. Let’s keep reading and see whether that guess holds up.
I’ve talked about the men for a while now, so let’s move on to a woman I actually like. Having read the first twenty chapters, my favorite character by far is the one known as “Sister Feng,” Wang Xi-feng.
Wang Xi-feng The moment Wang Xi-feng appears, she reads exactly like the type of extroverted older-sister figure who takes great care of her more introverted little sisters: she’s warm and affectionate with Dai-yu right from the start. She’s sharp-tongued and bold enough to call Grandmother Jia (her husband Jia Lian’s grandmother) “Old Ancestress.” She’s resourceful enough to scheme up a plan to punish the lecherous Jia Rui after he tries to make advances on her. She also has a gentle, proactive, caring side: when her close friend Ke-qing falls ill, she’s swamped with work and still makes time to visit and comfort her. She’s also a textbook case of “the capable one gets stuck doing everything”: not only does she run the day-to-day affairs of the Rong-guo mansion, but when trouble hits the Ning-guo mansion too, they call on her to handle that as well. It’s no wonder that the narrator of Dream of the Red Chamber, describing Xi-feng, praises her as spirited and dashing, a model of refined elegance.
I’ve been thinking that part of why I like this character so much might just be that everyone else looks so hopeless by comparison, lol, and it really makes her competence stand out. Also, her personality reminds me of certain extroverted “aunties” and “big sisters” who showed up in my life back when I was much more introverted myself: they were like little suns; just having them around was enough to evaporate all my nervousness and awkwardness.
I really hope Wang Xi-feng gets a good ending! But something tells me she won’t, ugh?
The Mirror That’s Impossible Not to Roast The “Mirror for the Romantic” is, well, a mirror. It shows up in Chapter 12, lent to Jia Rui by a lame Taoist priest when Jia Rui is dying of illness.
The lame Taoist tells him that if he looks into the back of the mirror, his illness will be cured within three days, but under no circumstances should he look into the front. Naturally, Jia Rui doesn’t listen. He looks into the back and sees a skeleton, and after the initial shock, he can’t resist the temptation and looks into the front instead, and there’s Wang Xi-feng, the woman he can’t stop thinking about. He climbs right into the mirror to be with her, and it ultimately costs him his life.
I told this story to Sam, and he said, doesn’t that sound exactly like one of those slightly useless gadgets from Doraemon? Or kind of like something Dr. Doofenshmirtz would invent, complete with a self-destruct button.
Fair point: this mirror really isn’t very user-friendly. If the whole point is to save someone’s life, why does it even need two sides? One side should be enough.
Sure, Jia Rui kind of brought it on himself, but I still think this “Mirror for the Romantic” gadget from the lame Taoist is honestly pretty useless too. I genuinely can’t tell if he was trying to save people or destroy them.
The Teetering Jia Household I remember finishing Chapter 4 and jotting down a note: why does it already feel like this household is on the verge of collapse? A few reasons: First, the family’s young men run wild outside, and the elders just quietly clean up after them without ever really disciplining them. Second, between the two Jia mansions, it somehow feels like Wang Xi-feng is the only woman actually holding things together. Third, the household servants cause trouble and show no respect for their masters. Fourth, when Yuan-chun, the consort living in the palace, comes home, she can’t help but sigh and shake her head, telling her family not to be so extravagant.
In Summary Overall, there have been a few things about this book that genuinely surprised me.
I’d heard people say the web of relationships in Dream of the Red Chamber is incredibly complicated, but having actually started reading, I’ve found it’s really not that hard to untangle. In Chapter 2, Cao Xueqin uses one of the characters to lay out a rough sketch of the entire family tree, and based on how he describes the relationships, you can actually go ahead and draft out a family tree for the Jia clan. Whenever a new character shows up later, the narrator is careful to clearly spell out how they’re related to everyone else. Once you’ve sketched it out on paper, you’re basically 70-80% of the way to understanding the whole thing.
On top of that, I originally assumed Cao Xueqin would save the Jia family’s decline for much later in the story, but as it turns out, right from the very beginning, he’s already been steadily laying the groundwork for a household full of cracks. I wonder where the next crack is going to show up. To find out what happens next, stay tuned for the next installment.
[Fun Vocabulary] Dream of the Red Chamber has some genuinely fun turns of phrase, so I wanted to collect a few here. Text in black is the book’s own explanation; orange text is my own take on the word.
Cuanduo (攛掇): to egg someone on, to instigate. Both characters have the “hand” radical, like someone poking another person, prodding them into doing something. Gousuiyaozhuo (詬誶謠諑): to insult and mock, to spread rumors and slander. Gou means to curse; sui means to scold; yao means rumor; zhuo means slander. All four characters share the “speech” radical, so reading it feels like someone endlessly running their mouth. “A hero among the rouge-and-powder set”: This is how Ke-qing describes Xi-feng. I find it delightful. I’d love to be a hero among the rouge-and-powder set myself. “A hero with piercing eyes”: refers to someone with sharp insight and outstanding intelligence. A pretty funny phrase: it makes me think of the Cyclops from The Odyssey. What is it like when Wisconsin’s AQI, usually somewhere in the 20s, spikes past 200?
Yesterday’s forecast said smoke from the Canadian wildfires was drifting straight over Wisconsin. Before bed, I turned the air purifier up to full blast.
I woke up this morning to a gray, hazy view outside, like morning fog that just never lifted all day. It was supposed to be a clear day, but the sky looked murky, like the water you rinse a paintbrush in.
My eyes felt dry, and my throat and nose were clogged with particles. My thoughts felt clogged too, sluggish and slow, my whole body felt heavy, and I had a bit of a headache on and off.
Meanwhile, my neighbors were out sunbathing. Some were grilling, some were even swimming.
I’m pretty sure their lungs are made of steel.
It’s fine, I’ll accept that I’m a hothouse flower, a cute little hothouse flower, haha.
I was just wondering today whether Marcus, who lives in Chicago, would put up a post about the air pollution, and sure enough, he did. Chicago’s AQI hit 500, so bad it seems almost off the scale. I hope everyone there is doing okay.

A friend was in Chicago on a business trip these past few days, so we made plans to meet up last Saturday and walked around Lincoln Park Zoo together.
We started at the outdoor lion area, but there wasn’t a single lion in sight. After wandering around for a while and circling back, we realized you could also view the lions from indoors, watching them through a glass window.
We walked into the indoor viewing area, turned a corner, and there they were: a male and a female lion. We got lucky and ended up in the front row, with only a pane of glass between us and the lions. As the crowd slowly gathered behind us, the two of them sauntered leisurely down from the fake rock formation. Then the king of beasts opened his jaws, baring his fangs with a fierce look, and the whole crowd gasped in awe.
I can’t remember if this was actually my first time seeing a lion, but it was definitely the closest I’ve ever been to one: his thick paws padding against the ground, his mane looking coarse and wonderfully full, his mouth opening to reveal sharp teeth, utterly majestic, and honestly kind of terrifying. I found myself with newfound respect for Daniel, who was thrown into the lions’ den. He wasn’t eaten, sure, but how did he not get scared to death?1
He circled around a few more times right in front of us, then suddenly stopped and lifted a leg. Shrieks and laughter erupted behind us at the same moment: yes, he was peeing, and aiming straight at the glass. If it hadn’t been for that pane of glass, I was standing close enough in the front row to have gotten sprayed head to toe (This moment, however precious, I let go unfilmed).
After the male lion finished his business, the female behind him walked down from the rock formation toward the dripping-wet glass. At the last critical second… she just sniffed it and walked away. Thank goodness she didn’t lick it, or the crowd behind me might have actually rioted.
My previous impression of lions came entirely from movies and cartoons: a mighty image I understood only in the abstract, without it ever feeling real. Actually visiting the zoo and seeing a real lion baring its teeth and claws right in front of me made me genuinely feel his presence and majesty, and I noticed goosebumps rising on my arms. That’s a reaction I could never have gotten just from understanding the concept of “lion” in my head.
Are there other things like this, things we know about only as concepts, but have never actually experienced? Maybe we all need to take an actual trip to the zoo sometime, and go see a real big kitty.

This is my submission for the “BlogBlog Club - June 2026.” This month’s theme is “Music and Memory,” hosted by Yoz. If you have your own blog, come join in! P.S. I only realized after finishing the draft that it happened to fit June’s theme perfectly, so I figured I’d submit it too!
I just got home from a concert, still riding the excitement and emotion of it, so I’m writing this down while it’s fresh.
This year marks the 100th anniversary of the founding of the MSO (Madison Symphony Orchestra), and Overture Hall opened its doors to the public for two days straight, with performances of all kinds of music running from morning to night, and all completely free. As local residents, of course we had to go be part of it!
We walked into the concert hall around four in the afternoon and were genuinely stunned by the crowd: it felt like the whole city was trying to squeeze in through that one small entrance (honestly, if this many people showed up on a regular day too, we wouldn’t have to worry about classical music going extinct). We got lucky and found seats dead center toward the back of the main floor, with great sightlines and great acoustics. The concert opened with George Gershwin’s An American in Paris. At first the orchestra seemed like it hadn’t quite woken up yet: this light, charming piece came out a little clumsy and hazy, but as the piece went on, the rhythm grew steadier and the musical expression grew richer.
The most stunning moment of the entire concert was the second piece, Pablo de Sarasate’s Carmen Fantasy for Violin and Orchestra, Op. 25! The solo was performed by Korean-American violinist Julian Rhee, and Rhee’s technique was honestly beyond words: he nailed some brutally difficult wide leaps with pinpoint precision, and his high notes were incredibly delicate. His whole body swayed with the music, and he looked like he was genuinely savoring every second of it. His performance was utterly magnetic. I kept my eyes glued to him the entire time, completely forgetting there was an entire orchestra behind him. Conductor John DeMain mentioned that Rhee, who was born in Milwaukee, won a music competition performing this very piece at age ten, pretty astonishing that someone so young could handle a piece with such demanding technique. His encore, Zigeunerweisen, came just as effortlessly. I have to say, Rhee, with his red-framed glasses, has an absolutely commanding stage presence.
The second half featured Gustav Holst’s The Planets, Suite for Large Orchestra, Op. 32, with four of the seven movements performed: Mars, Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter. Venus stuck with me the most; there’s a section with a main melody layered over repeating chords, building in a way that felt like watching a planet turn steadily on its axis, and I felt like I was floating right in front of Venus, watching it glow with a strange light in the quiet of space.
That sense of stillness got shattered during Jupiter, though to be fair, it wasn’t really the piece’s fault that it felt more chaotic than intended; it was the guy sitting behind me. About three minutes into the piece, a very familiar melody came in: the one used as background music in the Japanese drama Nodame Cantabile. And the guy behind me happily started humming along with the orchestra. If he’d at least been in tune, fine, but he was wildly off-key (facepalm), so I had to scoot forward a little, trying to salvage whatever notes had survived the massacre, scattered across the floor.
The concert closed with Beethoven’s Ninth. Conductor DeMain shared a story: once, after conducting the Ninth, an audience member told him afterward, “I thought it opened with the ‘Ode to Joy’ theme. I didn’t realize we’d have to wait three whole movements for it.”
“So, by popular demand, and also because we’re short on time, we’re only performing the fourth movement today,” he said, with a mischievous grin.
On the afternoon of December 29, 2019, Sam and I once heard the NSO perform the Ninth at the National Concert Hall (yes, I remember the exact date; I have a habit of writing things down). But there were no subtitles that time, so I only had a vague sense that it was a piece praising God. Today, with English subtitles projected in the hall, I finally understood the words more fully, and my heart and my head finally aligned on the same frequency at the same moment, resonating together into a shared sense of awe and reverence for God.
“Brothers, above the starry canopy a loving Father must dwell. Do you fall to your knees, you millions? World, do you sense your Creator?”
The melody built layer upon layer, voices soaring and rising, and as the very last note fell, the balloons that had been tied to the ceiling in all sorts of colors came showering down. The audience erupted in thunderous applause, and so many people kept batting the balloons back and forth, keeping them from touching the ground, as if that alone could stretch out the piece that had just ended, could let them hold on a little longer to a feeling that was already slipping away.
After the concert, the lobby had refreshments waiting: champagne and desserts that weren’t too sweet (the highest compliment a Taiwanese person can pay a dessert). Even with the crowd pressing in, some couples still took little dancing steps together, moving along with another ensemble performing nearby, and the festive energy in the lobby only kept building.
Will classical music disappear one day?
I don’t want to believe it will. Maybe that makes me one of those people batting the balloon too. But for now, in this moment, the balloon is still up in the air, hasn’t touched down yet, and I want to use my words to bat it just a little higher, keep it afloat just a little longer, let it drift all the way into your hands, your eyes, your ears: you, reading this.

This is my submission for the “BlogBlog Club - May 2026.” This month’s theme is “A Sentence That Changed How You See Life,” hosted by Eddie Lv. If you have your own blog, come join in!
My junior year of college, not long after I became a Christian, I was reading the Bible one day when I came across this line:
“You are precious and honored in my sight”
The context of that passage is God speaking to Israel: they belong to him, they need not fear outward hardship, because God is their God; and in his sight, the people of Israel are precious and honored.
I wasn’t very familiar with the Bible at the time and didn’t really understand the historical background or significance behind that passage. But as I kept reading, in that moment, for some reason, these words originally spoken to the nation of Israel felt like they were pointed straight at me, looking me in the eye.
I became the “you” in that sentence, and it was as if God were telling me, face to face: in his sight, I am precious and honored.
Part of me thought, “Okay, sure. So what?”
But another part of me felt something stir inside, as if something had been shaken loose. There are certainly people in my life I treasure, but I don’t think I’d ever describe any of them as “precious and honored.” And yet, in the eyes of the Creator (someone far greater than my teachers, my boss, the president, or the richest person alive), I was somehow precious, honored, and full of worth. That was hard to wrap my head around. But if it were true, would it mean my life held different possibilities than I’d assumed?
And whatever those different possibilities were, I figured, they were probably better than what I already had.
Ever since that sentence appeared, I’ve slowly come to realize that what got shaken loose was something I’d call “the theory that effort is what gives you value.” And I’ve come to understand that my original “okay, so what” reaction actually meant: if I don’t work hard, or if my effort doesn’t earn me some kind of result or worldly worth, then surely God wouldn’t feel this way about me, right?
Right?
As it turned out, over the years that followed, even in just the past year or two, there were times when I’d already poured every ounce of my heart and strength into facing certain people or doing certain things, and I still failed, and it was hard, in those moments, not to feel like worthless. And yet that sentence, “You are precious and honored in my sight,” kept haunting me, refusing to leave (using the word “haunting” might sound a bit weird, but it really does capture that feeling of something surfacing again and again, unbidden). That’s when I realized I’d had it wrong. God isn’t some player who abandons you the moment you’re down on your luck. Even when I was at my absolute lowest, his affection for me never expired: like a lover who only sees beauty in the one they love, in his eyes I was, and still am, someone precious.
Then, slowly, a new value system began to grow in place of the old “effort is what gives you value” one. I’d call this new one “I work hard because I already have value”: I don’t work hard in order to create my own worth, and I don’t work hard to earn a sense of security. I already possess a fixed worth that doesn’t fluctuate with my output, and working hard is simply what naturally flows out of me as a human being.
I have to say, this wasn’t something that grew purely out of my own willpower or reasoning. And it wasn’t as though hearing this one sentence instantly worked some kind of magic, flipping a switch on decades of old thought patterns. After all, changing yourself, or changing anyone, is an extraordinarily difficult thing. There’s an old Chinese saying: “Drag an ox all the way to Beijing, and it’s still an ox.” The change, as a whole, has been more like water wearing away stone, God’s patient, steady love gradually reshaping my temperament. My old value system had molded me into a very cranky, short-tempered ox, terrified that if the field didn’t produce anything, I’d be sold off and slaughtered. But this new value system lets me plow my field with a bit more calm and gentleness, and whatever does or doesn’t grow in that field, there’s no threat to my survival either way. I’m still, in God’s eyes, a perfectly lovable little moo.
That is the story behind “You are precious and honored in my sight.” This sentence was, in a way, tailor-made for me by God; it might not apply to you in quite the same way. But if you need a sentence of your own, I believe God already has one prepared; all you have to do is ask him for it, so why not give it a try? And if you’d ever like to talk about the Christian faith, feel free to reach out.

One day in early February, I was washing my glasses when I suddenly heard a crack: the left side of the frame snapped and the lens popped out.
These were acrylic round-frame glasses that had been with me for about ten years, the color faded from deep pink to pale pink over time, with rust marks showing along the temples. Well, I figured, it was time for them to retire. I glued the lens back in with some white glue as a stopgap and booked an appointment at a nearby optical shop (let’s call it Shop A).
Little did I know, that was only the opening act of the disaster to come. Before you read on, take a guess: how long do you think it took me to finally get a pair of glasses that worked properly? I’ll reveal the answer at the end.
I hadn’t gotten new glasses in ten years, and on top of that, this was my first time getting glasses in the US, so everything felt brand new. I walked into this shop that claimed to be the best in the country, without really noticing why there weren’t many customers inside. I went through some tests with the optometrist, then had an off-site doctor examine me remotely over a screen. I walked out of the exam room in high spirits and picked out frames. They happened to be on sale, so getting two pairs at once seemed like a good deal. I brought the frames to the counter to pay, and the cashier, radiating an air of low-energy world-weariness, casually quoted me a price way higher than expected. Sam and I both flinched. Wait, wasn’t this on sale? She went “oh” and said that price was for the cheapest lenses; given how strong my prescription was, I’d need thinner lenses, which cost more.
All the pricing lived on her computer, and there was no printed price list I could check for myself, so I just told her a budget. Her fingers clacked away rapidly on the keyboard, and a new number came out of her mouth. That one was borderline acceptable. Glasses are a necessity, after all, so I just paid up.
“How long until the new glasses are ready?” “Two weeks. We’ll text you when they’re done.”
Fine, I figured: this is America, after all. If calling customer service is slow here, getting glasses made is probably slow too. I’d just have to be patient.
Two weeks later, I got a text saying the glasses were ready for pickup. The text also said: “We are closing down soon. Please come pick up your order by 2/28. For any questions after that, please contact our other branch.”
I rushed over to Shop A to pick them up. A lot of the shelves inside were already cleared out, the optometrist was nowhere to be seen, and only that same cashier from before remained, her low-energy world-weariness seemingly even more pronounced under the harsh fluorescent lights. I tried on the new glasses and immediately felt dizzy and disoriented. Well, I figured, my body probably just needed time to adjust. I gritted my teeth and took the glasses home.
After several days of trying hard to adjust, something still felt very wrong: putting the glasses on made me dizzy every single time, I couldn’t read for long, my left eye was constantly out of focus, and the frame was clamped too tight, pressing painfully on my temples. I finally dragged Sam along to another branch to deal with these two new pairs of glasses. This branch, let’s call it A’, was quite far from home, a good thirty-plus minute drive. Not wanting to make the trip for nothing, I booked an appointment with a doctor there online in advance.
At branch A’, I ran into the same optometrist from before; apparently she’d been transferred there. She rattled on about how the axis might be off, though she wasn’t entirely sure, and said the doctor would take a look at me shortly. This branch actually had an in-house doctor, so at least she wasn’t on a screen this time, though her leg was in a cast, and she hobbled me into the exam room on crutches, not looking particularly pleased. She seemed like she wanted to brush me off with a few quick words at first, but after I persisted and explained how much trouble these two pairs of glasses had caused me, she silently retested my vision without explaining why I’d been dizzy. I had to keep politely pressing for an explanation before she finally said it might be because the prescription between my two eyes was too different, and that she’d adjusted it to bring them closer together this time, hopefully improving the dizziness. I took the new prescription and asked the front desk to remake the lenses, and also asked them to loosen the frame a bit.
So I waited, and waited, another two weeks, and finally got the text that my order was ready. We drove half an hour to A’, and the man at the counter pulled just one pair out from the back shelf. I asked, “Where’s the other one? I ordered two pairs.” He said, “Oh, our policy is we only start on the second pair once the first one’s confirmed to be right. The other pair still needs another two weeks.”
In that moment, my last nerve didn’t snap; it reconnected. Suddenly I could see every single absurd, unreasonable thing about this place with total clarity, and my “be nice” mode switched off, replaced by “reasonably angry” mode. I told the guy, you never mentioned this to us before: it takes us an hour round trip to get to this shop, and now we have to make another trip. He apologized, not very sincerely, then offered to just ship the second pair to our house instead, though, he added, we’d have to cover the shipping cost. (Do you hear yourself right now?)
Fuming, I took the pair they had and went straight home. Wearing them, I got dizzy all over again, and the frame that used to be too tight was now too loose. I took them off to examine them closely and discovered the lens technician had literally shaved off a corner where the temple meets the lens! Yes, shaved it off: the kind of damage you can’t undo.
My anger cooled into sheer exhaustion. Sam and I talked it over: it had already been over a month, and the pair I now had still wasn’t wearable, and there was still another pair to wait on. Given this shop’s customer service and craftsmanship, I could easily picture having to make yet another trip to get things adjusted even after picking up the second pair. Round and round, when would it ever end? After thinking it over for a few days, I decided to cut my losses, took the glasses back, and returned them for a refund, including the pair that wasn’t even finished yet. I got my money back for the glasses, though I couldn’t get a refund on the doctor’s exam fee. But that was fine. My time and energy really needed an immediate stop-loss.
After leaving Shop A, I did some serious research and found a different optical shop with much better reviews (let’s call it Shop B) which offered an online glasses-ordering service: you fill in your prescription on the website, and they ship the glasses straight to your door. There was also a physical location just ten minutes from our place for any adjustments. Not wanting to spend even more money on another eye exam, I decided to just try using the prescription from A’. As luck would have it, the delivery date happened to land on the exact day I was flying back to Taiwan. While I was at the airport, Sam took photos at home and texted me: “I think the quality on this one is so much better!” Just the glasses case alone was nothing like Shop A’s cheap, low-quality clear plastic box. This one had a hard black shell with a spring hinge that popped open or snapped shut with the lightest touch, lined inside with soft, skin-toned microfiber. It felt genuinely premium, and the glasses looked pretty impressive sitting inside it.
Three weeks later, back in the US, I finally got to put the new glasses on. The overall quality from Shop B was clearly much better than either A or A’. The only downside was that I still got dizzy; it just took longer to kick in. I thought about it and realized that since I need to read and write for long stretches, I really couldn’t settle for “good enough.” So I booked an appointment with Shop B’s doctor and decided to get my prescription checked all over again, from scratch.
Shop B was bustling and had a cheerful atmosphere, and even with plenty of customers, the staff still managed to take good care of everyone. The optometrist ran her tests, looked over the two prescriptions I had in hand, and said, “Ah, so you’re looking for a second opinion?” Then she looked again. “Oh wait, no, these first two are from the same shop, but two different doctors. You’re actually looking for a third opinion.”
The doctor then strolled in, calm and unhurried, a relaxed-looking older gentleman. The optometrist relayed my situation to him while he listened and asked me questions along the way. As I aired my grievances about the other shop, he kept dishing out sympathy in full measure: “Oh no!” He carefully explained my situation, saying the other shop had probably over-corrected my astigmatism, that overly strong astigmatism correction was likely the source of my dizziness, and that what I actually needed was a pair of glasses that felt comfortable, with a prescription close to my original one.
“We’re not going to be like that other shop,” the doctor said, with real conviction.
When I went to pay, I asked the front desk how long it would take. The short-haired young lady answered with confident pride: “Within the hour!”
And sure enough, in under an hour, I got a text saying: “Your glasses are ready! We got it done in just 24 minutes!”
Once I put them on, my vision snapped into focus and, finally, no dizziness. The front desk staff, who by then knew all about my absurd ordeal, looked genuinely relieved seeing the satisfied smile on my face. I walked out of that shop feeling like I’d stepped into a different world, wandering through the nearby shopping street under the noon sun to test the glasses out: no dizziness. I walked into the bookstore next door to test them under the dim lighting: no headache either. From walking into that shop last Monday for the exam to finally getting my new glasses, the whole thing took barely two hours total.
Did you get the question from the start of this post right? I picked up my glasses last Monday, and my very first appointment was back in early February, over three months in total.
Truly absurd. I’m recording it here for everyone’s entertainment, and maybe as a cautionary tale too: if you want a bright future ahead of you, choose your optical shop wisely.

It has been more than half a year since this blog went live, and along with some shifts in my life, I made a few adjustments to bring the blog more in line with where I am now and what I want from it.
The most visible change is the new site favicon. Ever since I developed tendinitis in both hands at the end of last year, I haven’t been able to play piano for very long. At its worst, just five minutes of playing would leave my hands stiff and numb, and there was a stretch where seeing my piano would actually make me sad. I don’t make my living from music (does that mean I can still call myself a musician? hmm), but playing piano and making music has always been core to who I am, and I found that identity colliding with my physical limitations like two tectonic plates grinding against each other, the pressure building the whole time.
I decided to take that tag off the homepage first, and off my heart, too, for a while, and focus on other interesting things instead.
After thinking it over, I decided to redo the site’s favicon. I opened the Sketchbook app on my iPad and, in about five seconds, sketched out a pencil doodle,1 originally meaning to go back and add more detail. But when I sat back and looked at it, I suddenly realized the sketch was just too cute as it was: those unintentional, imperfect lines weren’t something AI could replicate, and honestly, I couldn’t draw the exact same thing twice myself either. Maybe you could say the roughness of the lines represents the author of this site speaking loosely and casually, and if that’s the case, I’d ask you, the reader, to read it just as loosely and casually too. lol
Next I rewrote the “About” page. Honestly, “About” might be the hardest page on the entire blog to write. Beyond privacy concerns, it also comes loaded with all kinds of overthinking: if I write about my career, will readers just see me through the lens of that career? If I write about my personality, what if the personality I think I have doesn’t match what readers actually perceive? Should I even bother writing it then? Plenty of fellow bloggers skip the “About” page entirely, and some readers/bloggers, like Tian-Yan, prefer to just read the posts and piece together their own impression of the author from there. Still, even though not every reader will click through to “About,” I really wanted there to be one, since I’m genuinely curious how every writer chooses to describe themselves. To satisfy that little reader living in my head, I mulled it over for ages, until it suddenly hit me: hey, if describing myself directly feels like too much pressure, why not just describe how I think about writing and about this platform instead? Those thoughts are, after all, the meta-reflection behind every post I write, and the whole reason this site exists in the first place. That felt right, so I gave it a major rewrite.
While revising, I also went back through old posts I’d written, and it was oddly fascinating. My writing really has changed, and my voice seems to be slowly finding its own shape. On top of that, a few other little shoots and buds have sprouted too: learning different ways to express myself;
learning to find deeper meaning in the small, boring stuff;
practicing how to voice my opinions in a public space;
and learning to keep my own inner motivation going without outside feedback (I completely agree with what Marcus says: don’t measure it).
Beyond all that, there’s also been a happy accident: the website VisBible.org.
That site only exists because this blog came first. I’d originally wanted to put the notes I casually make while reading the Bible (image below) up on the blog for others to reference. Without the blog, I probably wouldn’t even have had the idea to share them at all. But there are plenty of people who make images like that, and comparatively few who build whole websites for it, so why not just build a website?
(A timeline of the kings in the Book of Kings)
Turns out I had dug myself a huge hole, but I am having so much fun down here.
That’s more or less my reflection after half a year (seven months, technically) of blogging. There have been some adjustments, and some surprises both expected and unexpected. I hope I can keep writing, digging myself out of the ground a little bit more each time.

The day before flying back to the States, my family and I went to Yangmingshan to see the calla lilies.
I had only ever visited Qingtiangang Grassland there before. Yangmingshan’s flower fields have a well-known reputation, and though I had long wanted to go, the timing never quite worked out. Getting to go this time with family made it all the more special.
We took the MRT to Jiantan Station, then hopped on the S8 bus all the way up to Zhuzihu. On the way back, the S8 was full, so we switched to the S9 and rode it down to Beitou MRT Station instead. All in all, getting there and back was quite straightforward.
Stepping off the bus, a cool mountain breeze swept right into us. The temperature up in the hills was noticeably lower than in the city, making it a wonderful escape from the heat. A short walk brought us to the calla lily fields. The fields are privately owned, so there’s an entrance fee, but at 100 NTD it’s very reasonable, and the ticket can be exchanged for five calla lilies or three irises, which makes it an excellent deal.
Though they’re called fields, they feel more like paddies, with the flowers blooming right out of the water. We went on a Monday, so it wasn’t crowded at all, and we could take photos freely, surrounded by hills and flowers. It really did feel like a world apart. The bees there were wonderfully plump and round, each little glutton diving headfirst into a calla lily or iris, stuffing itself in nose-first with its bottom wriggling in after, utterly absorbed. Genuinely the most endearing thing.
The calla lilies were what drew us there, but it was the bees that made the flowers even more beautiful. The lilies showed me how strange and wonderful a petal’s shape and angle of bloom can be. The bees let me smell flowers’ sweetness. I’ve always found it odd that the Chinese expression for “attracting bees and butterflies” (招蜂引蝶) carries a negative connotation. To me, a flower visited by bees feels warmer and more alive, less aloof, more approachable. And since every flower will fade in the end, why not bloom boldly and joyfully? Why wither in quiet, solitary dignity?
The power of “togetherness” is greater than we think. Talking with my family, I said that Yangmingshan isn’t actually far at all, and yet on my own I could never quite summon the motivation to go up and see the flowers. So why does having someone alongside make it so much easier? Some things seem to work that way. Alone, the same thing feels flat. With one other person, it comes alive. With two, it becomes a garden in full bloom.1
The season is winding down. Go see the flowers, and bring someone with you.

posts.text:
A few weeks ago, back in Taiwan, a friend asked me:
“After all these years away, how do you think you’ve changed?”
I thought for a moment and said, “I think it’s this feeling of being a stranger everywhere, no matter where I am.”
The conversation drifted on, but my thoughts stayed behind. Three weeks earlier, landing at Taoyuan Airport, walking from the plane through the jet bridge, the familiar humid heaviness hit my skin all at once, and memories began pressing themselves back, one by one. Strangely, though, they wouldn’t quite stick. The distance that had grown between me and Taiwan over these years in the States had apparently given my body some kind of non-stick coating.
And yet I wasn’t sad about it. I didn’t think the distance was a bad thing. If anything, I finally understood something about my past self.
How so?
After living somewhere quiet for a few years, I came to realize that life in Taiwan had always kept my senses in a state of constant overload:
the grinding shriek of train wheels rounding the curve between Dongmen and Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall MRT stations; the suffocating stillness just before an afternoon thunderstorm breaks; pedestrians darting across streets without a glance at the crosswalk; the firecrackers and piercing suona horns of a temple procession winding through the neighborhood; the night markets blazing with signs in screaming colors and clashing contrasts,
and countless other experiences I could never quite catalogue, all of which left me thoroughly worn out. I always wondered why most of the people around me seemed to manage just fine, rolling with the noise, joining in the gossip. I had grown up on this same soil, yet somehow never grew the eyes, nose, or ears to match it. (My mouth, however, adapted beautifully. Taiwanese food is unbeatable.)
Leaving that land for North America, I found streets that were calmer, more harmonious in color, neighborhoods where houses sat in quiet order. But there was plenty here that demanded its own kind of adjustment: customer service calls that route you through number after number before leaving you on hold for half an hour; a two or three hour drive counted as nearby; restaurant servers who interrupt your meal to check on you, and then you tip them on top of it. (How is everything tasting? Great, thank you. How is everything tasting? Great, thank you. How is everything tasting? Great, thank you.)
Do I miss Taiwan desperately because of all this? Not entirely. Do I miss the States desperately when I’m back in Taiwan? Not entirely either. I suddenly understood what a classmate once told me: “I’ve now lived in the States longer than I lived back home. I’m always missing Sri Lanka when I’m in America, and missing America when I’m in Sri Lanka.”
Which leads me to a hypothesis: what if home is simply the sum of everything we miss? Home no longer confined to a birthplace or a childhood address, but stretched across time, made of the people, places, and things our hearts are tied to. Or perhaps it doesn’t even need to be something we love deeply. Just somewhere we can exist without feeling out of place, somewhere we fit rather than merely tolerate, is already remarkable. In this wide world, in environments that so often make us feel like we don’t quite belong, finding even one or two spaces where we can simply rest and breathe is an extraordinary stroke of luck.
Writing this, I find myself thinking of the family and friends scattered in different places. Why do we become family and friends to each other? If it were purely biology, then by my own definition,1 some people who share my blood don’t really fall within what I’d call family. If it were shared interests, how many interests does it take to truly become a friend? Does any common interest qualify? If it were shared values, then why do we sometimes meet people who are better than us in ways that make us willing to change?
And sometimes, if we had met the same person at a different point in their life, or ours, perhaps we wouldn’t have become friends at all. So why is it that meeting someone at a particular moment can determine, for the rest of a lifetime, whether they become family or friend?
The answer feels too mysterious for me to fully grasp. For now, I can only call it grace. Because this is not something we can get through effort, or arrange by carefully scheduling the right encounters. The grace of meeting someone who fits, someone with whom we simply belong, is what allows us, wherever we end up, to catch a glimpse of home: no loneliness, no need to stay guarded, time together that passes like seconds, old unspoken understandings quietly growing into new ones.
And it is somewhere in that accumulation of seconds and unspoken understanding that the overwhelming sensory experiences and the cultural frustrations suddenly become a little easier to bear. I’m grateful that some people in my life have become a place I can rest when I’m tired. And I’m honored to be that place for some of them in return.
May we be home to one another.
NB: This article was first published in Chinese on 04/18/26. It was later translated with assistance from AI tools, edited by me, and published in English on 05/02/26.
“Family” here refers to the subset of people, within both biological and faith relationships, with whom I genuinely feel at ease. “Friends” refers not only to peers but more broadly to those across all ages with whom I share a sincere connection. These definitions are not objective truths that apply universally; they are simply the author’s personal sense of things. ↩︎

At the library near my house, I spotted a slim little book sitting in the non-fiction section called “How to Save Time.”
I was expecting it to be a straightforward book — some arguments, maybe a few practical tips. But the moment I opened to the first page, I was stunned.
The first page: ……Okay?
I flipped through it quickly. The whole book was exactly like the first page: one picture and one simple sentence.
“May keeps losing her things.” “So May put a bowl on the table. The bowl holds her glasses. The bowl holds her keys. The bowl holds her phone.” “Now May knows where things are.”
……So May had been wasting all her time looking for her stuff this whole time?
There was also this part:
“May wants to do it all.” “She takes classes.” “She bowls on a team.” “She helps at a playschool.” “But May cannot do it all.” “So May cuts down.” “She saves time.”
……Life could really be that simple, couldn’t it lol
The thing that made me nearly lose it in the library was this: (What does this have to do with saving time?!) I screamed internally, desperately trying not to laugh in the library, shoulders shaking the whole time.
You shouldn’t chase productivity too hard in life. Proper rest is still necessary. That’s what the author was trying to say, right?
If you’re curious, feel free to grab a copy here — $9.95 each, and there’s a preview on the website. Oh, and by the way, the audio sample is actually long enough that you can hear the entire book.
